# What Is Conversion Rate Optimization, and When to Do It

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-conversion-rate-optimization/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-05 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Growth

> Summary: Conversion rate optimisation increases the share of visitors who sign up, apply, fund, buy or book, through diagnosis, hypothesis, testing and measurement. Baymard's checkout research shows how much loss comes from fixable friction. It needs enough traffic to test, the conversion the business actually runs on, and the right visitors; if the visitors were never going to buy, the problem is upstream.

Conversion rate optimisation (CRO) is the work of finding what stops suitable visitors from taking a useful action, changing it for a reason and checking whether the change helped. Much of the loss is friction rather than reluctance: Baymard Institute finds 70.22% of online carts are abandoned, and among the reasons shoppers give, unexpected extra costs lead at 40%. CRO needs the right success metric, enough traffic to test honestly, and visitors who were plausible buyers in the first place.

Your website is attracting visitors, but too few are signing up, booking a call or completing an application. Before spending more money bringing people in, it makes sense to ask what is stopping the people already there. That is the job of CRO.

## CRO is not changing the button colour

A typical process is simple: look at where visitors leave, talk to customers or review support questions, form a hypothesis and test a specific improvement. You might simplify an application, explain a confusing fee or make the next step clearer on a mobile screen.

A new design can help, but a prettier page is not proof of better conversion. Neither is a temporary spike in sign-ups after a small edit. The discipline is in the sequence: evidence of a problem, a stated reason for the change, and a measurement plan agreed before anyone looks at results.

## Optimise the action the business actually needs

Imagine a hypothetical fintech app whose landing page converts more visitors into sign-ups after a redesign. That looks promising until the team discovers that fewer of those users fund their accounts. If the business earns revenue from active funded customers, the measure cannot stop at registration.

| Business | Easy conversion to report | Conversion the business runs on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Consumer fintech | Registrations | Accounts that pass identity checks and fund |
| Enterprise software | Demo form fills | Qualified demos that become opportunities |
| Developer platform | Sign-ups | Successful first integrations |
| Commerce | Orders | Orders not refunded or returned |

The right conversion sits as close to revenue as you can measure in a reasonable time. A useful frame is three questions in order: are the visitors looking for a problem this product solves (attract); can they understand the offer and complete the next meaningful step (activate); and do new customers keep using the product or reach the intended outcome (retain)? Our piece on [what a marketing funnel is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-marketing-funnel/) covers how to find which of those stages is the constraint.

## Look for confusion before assuming people need persuasion

Start with analytics that show the path through the product, and pair those numbers with what users report. Do support tickets mention unclear pricing? Do people abandon a form when asked for identity documents? Is the mobile page too slow to use?

Baymard Institute's checkout research shows how much of the loss is friction. Its average documented cart abandonment rate is 70.22%, the mean of 50 studies published between 2006 and 2025. After excluding shoppers who were just browsing, US shoppers in Baymard's survey gave these reasons:

| Reason for abandoning during checkout | Share of US shoppers |
| --- | --- |
| Extra costs too high (shipping, tax, fees) | 40% |
| Delivery too slow | 20% |
| Did not trust the site with card details | 19% |
| Site required account creation | 18% |
| Checkout too long or complicated | 17% |
| Website errors or crashes | 17% |
| Could not see or calculate total cost up front | 12% |

Every row except delivery speed is a design or disclosure problem. Baymard estimates the average large ecommerce site could raise conversion by 35.26% through better checkout design, while noting such gains "won't come easy". Retail checkouts are not B2B forms, but the pattern carries: hidden costs, forced steps and unexplained requests lose people who intended to act.

For a regulated product, explain why personal information is required and what happens next. Make fees, eligibility and important conditions easy to understand. Clarity can reduce wasted applications as well as increase qualified ones.

A useful hypothesis is specific: "Applicants may leave at the identity-check step because the page does not explain why the information is needed." That is easier to investigate than "the landing page needs to convert better."

> Conversion work is powerful when qualified people meet unnecessary friction. It cannot turn irrelevant traffic into customers.

## Two kinds of evidence: observation and experiment

**Usability testing finds problems.** Jakob Nielsen's analysis for Nielsen Norman Group found the first five test users reveal about 85% of usability problems, and recommended several small rounds with fixes in between rather than one large study. It works at any traffic level, and it tells you why people struggle. It does not tell you how much a fix will lift conversion.

**A/B testing measures effects.** An A/B test compares experiences to see whether a change improves an outcome. It needs a sample size and a measurement plan chosen before the test starts. As a rough illustration from the standard two-proportion formula, a page converting at 3% needs on the order of 14,000 visitors per variation to detect a 20% relative lift (to 3.6%) at 95% confidence and 80% power. Smaller effects need far more. Use a sample-size calculator with your own assumptions rather than declaring a winner after a few dozen visits.

Do not stop a test the moment it looks significant. Evan Miller's widely cited analysis showed that checking for significance after every observation and stopping at the first 5% result produces false positives 26.1% of the time, more than five times the stated rate. Fix the sample size in advance, or use a sequential or Bayesian method designed for repeated looks. If a test is inconclusive, say so, and use what you learned to sharpen the next hypothesis. Our piece on [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers test design in more depth.

| Situation | Method | What it can claim |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Low traffic, clear friction | Usability test with five users, fix, repeat | Problems found and removed |
| High traffic, specific hypothesis | A/B test with planned sample size | Measured lift, with confidence |
| Either, with ambiguous results | Report as inconclusive | A refined next hypothesis |

## CRO cannot fix the wrong audience

If almost nobody visits a page, the team may not have enough data for a meaningful A/B test. It can still fix confusing forms, missing disclosures or broken mobile layouts through observation and review. Those are sensible fixes, not statistically proven lifts, and should be reported that way.

If most visitors were never likely to buy, fix the audience, offer or acquisition channel first. The economics matter here too: a conversion gain that comes from discounting or loosening qualification can raise acquisition numbers while lengthening [CAC payback](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-cac-payback/).

## lowob takeaways

- **Find the blocker first.** Investigate what confuses or stops suitable visitors before redesigning.
- **Use the conversion the business runs on.** Funded accounts and qualified demos, not registrations.
- **Be honest about evidence.** Observation finds problems; experiments measure effects; neither should be dressed as the other.
- **Fix acquisition when necessary.** CRO cannot rescue a page filled with the wrong audience.

## Common questions

### What is conversion rate optimisation in simple terms?

It is improving the share of visitors who take a valuable action, such as buying, booking or applying, by finding what stops them, changing it for a stated reason and measuring the result.

### How much traffic do you need for A/B testing?

It depends on your baseline rate and the lift you want to detect. As a rough guide, a 3% conversion rate needs around 14,000 visitors per variation to detect a 20% relative lift with standard settings. Low-traffic sites should rely on usability testing.

### What are the most common reasons people abandon a checkout?

In Baymard Institute's survey of US shoppers, unexpected extra costs led at 40%, followed by slow delivery, distrust of the site with card details, forced account creation and long or complicated checkouts.

### When is CRO a waste of time?

When the visitors are the wrong audience, when traffic is too low to test and the team treats small samples as proof, or when the metric being optimised is not the one the business earns from.
